content: 1. The document titled Quality Standards of Practice for National HIV Estimation Models was accessed on June 27, 2022. It provides a framework for ensuring the accuracy and reliability of HIV epidemic modeling at the district level in sub-Saharan Africa. 2. The Naomi model, developed by Eaton JW, Dwyer-Lindgren L, Gutreuter S, O'Driscoll M, Stevens O, Bajaj S, and others, is a tool designed to estimate HIV epidemic indicators at the district level in sub-Saharan Africa. This model was detailed in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2021. 3. Digital health systems must explicitly incorporate interoperability standards, data use rules, and transparent governance to enable secure exchange and utilization of health data. This includes the use of technical, organizational, and legal standards to facilitate data sharing and governance among healthcare partners. 4. Health ministries, partners, and civil society should publish agreed-upon standards, rules, and frameworks for data use to enhance transparency, data sharing, and utilization. 5. Unique identifiers should replace personal information with anonymous alphanumeric codes to support person-centered data management across facilities, districts, and health programs. These identifiers must preserve individual anonymity and separate personal data from routinely shared health data. 6. Unique identifiers should be progressively introduced across healthcare systems to promote person-centered services. National technical and legal protections must be adopted to safeguard these identifiers and allow individuals access to their associated data. 7. Investments in secure and confidential data systems are essential. These systems should have varying levels of data security based on healthcare needs and user roles, such as caregivers, implementers, health ministries, and civil society. 8. Personal data must remain confidential and accessible only to the data subject and explicitly authorized parties. Unauthorized disclosure of personal data is strictly prohibited. 9. The exponential growth in health data necessitates systematic investment in digital healthcare systems. This transition from paper-based to digital systems offers significant opportunities to improve health outcomes but also poses risks, particularly in the context of HIV and communicable diseases. 10. The success of digital health systems depends on appropriate governance strategies and policies that protect healthcare data and individual rights. Person-centered data requires consultation with the data subject in the design and implementation of digital systems. 11. Digitization of health data can improve patient outcomes by enhancing healthcare system responsiveness, enabling real-time data use, and facilitating seamless data sharing across facilities and agencies. 12. Patients should have access to their health data through portable, protected personal health records. Over time, person-centered data should empower individuals to shape how their data is used. 13. The digital divide refers to the gap between those who can access digital services and those who cannot. This divide may limit access to health services, personal health data, and educational resources. Factors contributing to the divide include cost, digital literacy, and perceived irrelevance of internet access. 14. Digital health systems must address equity to ensure that increased digitization does not exacerbate healthcare inequalities. Consideration should be given to those with limited digital connectivity or literacy. 15. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed resources to guide the implementation of digital health systems, including the Digital Implementation Investment Guide, the Global Strategy on Digital Health 2020–2025, and recommendations on digital interventions for health system strengthening. 16. WHO's SMART guidelines aim to support the digitization of health information systems. These guidelines are standards-based, machine-readable, adaptive, requirements-based, and testable, with five layers ranging from narrative guidelines to dynamic precision health models. 17. The Prevention Adaptive Learning and Management System (PALMS) in Blantyre, Malawi, integrates and analyzes data to support decision-making along the HIV prevention cascade. This system was developed using a user-centered design approach to ensure it meets the needs of its users. 18. User-centered design (UCD) involves extensive user interviews and continuous feedback loops to ensure that digital systems are user-friendly and reduce the burden on healthcare workers. It is critical for fostering trust and adoption of digital health systems.
